(Iran International, 19 Nov 2026)

Trump has not made a decision but is weighing Israeli intelligence warnings that Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals, according to the report.

The newspaper reported that the discussions intensified last week when Mossad director Roman Gofman visited Washington and met with senior US officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Other senior Israeli intelligence officials have also advocated renewed military operations against Iran.

According to the report, a senior Israeli official disputed the characterization that Netanyahu had pressured Trump.

The report said deep divisions remain within the Trump administration over the strength of the intelligence and whether another major offensive is justified, particularly following midterm elections in which voters expressed dissatisfaction with the war.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Dan Caine have presented Trump with military options developed by US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper, according to the newspaper.

Potential targets include Iran's missile and drone arsenals, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) command centers and energy facilities. Israeli planning has also included further attacks on Iranian nuclear sites and widespread strikes on energy infrastructure that could disrupt electricity supplies to industries and civilians, an option Trump has not agreed to.

“The US military continues to provide the president options, and all options remain on the table,” the Pentagon said in a statement to the newspaper.

The report said the US military had assembled substantial firepower in the region, including aircraft carriers, fighter jets and bombers. Long-range B-1 and B-2 bombers based in the United States have been on 96-hour notice for potential missions against Iran.

The Pentagon and State Department have also withdrawn personnel from regional bases and facilities as a precaution against renewed fighting, while the US recently delivered an additional Patriot antimissile battery to Israel, according to the report.

Trump recently instructed Vice President JD Vance to abandon efforts to negotiate a settlement with Tehran and has considered maintaining economic pressure to push Iran into an agreement to give up its nuclear program.

The newspaper reported that Netanyahu's push for renewed strikes comes as he leads a caretaker government following Israel's October election, with opposition parties seeking to form a coalition. Renewed fighting could complicate those efforts and potentially strengthen his political position.

Listen to this article100%FILE PHOTO: Iranian missiles are displayed at the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force Museum in Tehran, Iran, November 12, 2025.US officials warned Wednesday of Iranian threats against Americans and sanctioned Tehran-linked networks, while Iranian officials threatened regional oil infrastructure, missile strikes and revenge for Ali Khamenei's killing.

In written testimony submitted to the House Homeland Security Committee, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia accused Iran of espionage, cyber operations and plots against American officials and dissidents, citing 18 Iran-related counterintelligence and espionage arrests since President Donald Trump returned to office.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned that Iranian cyber operatives increasingly targeted US transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also described a substantial increase in threats from Iran, particularly plots targeting Americans at home and abroad.

Washington's response extended to Iran's regional financial networks, with the Treasury Department sanctioning a Hezbollah-linked charity and a gold-and-cash smuggling network in Lebanon and Turkey.

The department said the network transferred funds from the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force to Lebanon on Hezbollah's behalf, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pledged continued action against Tehran's financing operations.

Iranian officials warn of retaliation and wider attacks

In Tehran, officials issued a series of threats of their own. The Intelligence Ministry said it was awaiting an opportunity to avenge the killing of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other Iranian officials, while Ahmadreza Pourkhaghan, head of the armed forces' judicial organization, called for identifying and targeting US and Israeli military bases in the region.

The warnings extended to Iran's missile capabilities. Deputy Basij chief Ghasem Ghoreishi said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had ordered the armed forces to extend their missile range, while Army Chief Amir Hatami warned of a stronger response to “adversaries' mistakes.”

Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for parliament's national security committee, went further, saying: “Today, the enemy does not know on which continent the Islamic Republic’s missiles will land.” He also dismissed the prospect of concessions to Washington.

Earlier Wednesday, the US military warned that vessels receiving Iranian cargo through ship-to-ship transfers could face seizure or other enforcement action under Washington's naval blockade.

Deputy Parliament Speaker Hamidreza Haji Babaei turned his attention to regional energy infrastructure, calling for attacks on oil pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

He argued that other countries should be prevented from exporting oil while Iran's exports remained blocked and threatened energy facilities in countries allowing attacks on Iran from their territory.

Wednesday's developments reflected an increasingly confrontational exchange, with Washington targeting Iranian security and financial networks while Tehran threatened to expand the geographic reach and economic consequences of any renewed conflict.

Listen to this article100%A member of the Iraqi armed group Kataib Hezbollah looks on from a vehicle in Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 17, 2026. REUTERSIraq's army was awaiting orders Wednesday to take control of a stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah south of Baghdad, as reports emerged that IRGC Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani had met Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to help defuse the escalating standoff.

“The army is awaiting zero hour to move and take control of the area of Jurf al-Sakhar,” Defense Ministry spokesperson Yahya Rasool said, according to Lebanese newspaper An-Nahar, adding that the operation would follow a plan approved by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.

Rasool said security forces were coordinating their efforts and expressed hope that the operation would proceed without confrontation. According to the Defense Ministry, the army would protect energy transmission lines and help displaced residents return to the area, provided they were not wanted by judicial or security authorities.

Earlier Wednesday, Iraq's armed forces command approved a plan to deploy army, federal police and Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) units to take control of Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah. Under the plan, an army brigade, a federal police brigade and two PMF brigades would each take responsibility for a sector, while energy police would secure oil pipelines.

The planned deployment follows a warning Tuesday from Kataib Hezbollah that it would confront government forces if they attempted to enter Jurf al-Sakhar, which the group has controlled for more than a decade.

“If a war is imposed on us we will fight,” a Kataib Hezbollah official told journalists visiting the area, according to the Associated Press.

The standoff poses a test of Zaidi's efforts to bring Iran-backed armed groups under state control, amid concerns about possible fighting.

Two Kataib Hezbollah officials told AP Tuesday that Qaani, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help mediate the dispute between the militia and Iraqi authorities.

Iraqi Kurdish outlet Rudaw reported Wednesday, citing two senior Iraqi officials, that Qaani met Zaidi on Monday night and was told the militia must withdraw peacefully or face intervention by Iraqi security forces.

The tensions intensified after Iraqi authorities launched an investigation into allegations that Kataib Hezbollah had used Jurf al-Sakhar, in Babil province about 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad, to smuggle oil worth tens of millions of dollars.

Iraqi lawmaker Ali Anhair told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) that investigators reviewed documents and surveillance footage showing about 25 tanker trucks, each capable of carrying 36,000 liters of oil.

“The reports reviewed by the committee were shocking and included evidence and documents proving the existence of smuggling operations in Jurf al-Nasr, supported by photographs, videos and footage captured by drones,” he said.

Authorities also dismissed nine security and administrative officials and referred suspects to the judiciary.

Kataib Hezbollah denied the smuggling allegations. An official from the group told journalists visiting Jurf al-Sakhar on Tuesday that two facilities in the area refined oil solely to fuel its vehicles and electricity generators, AP reported.

The United States has backed efforts to disarm Iran-backed militias in Iraq as part of its broader push to reduce Tehran's regional influence. The United States designated Kataib Hezbollah as a foreign terrorist organization in 2009.

Listen to this article100%File photo: The Karun-4 Dam on the Karun River in southwestern Iran.Iranian officials have seized on a controversial New York Times report about the possible military use of dams to broaden their threats of retaliation against US and Israeli infrastructure.

The November 16 report, titled “War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason,” raised the possibility that some Iranian water projects could support underground missile bases, citing geographical similarities between the projects and missile sites targeted in US and Israeli strikes.

The newspaper emphasized that the alleged connection remained speculative. But the report prompted a backlash on social media, with users and some experts accusing the newspaper and its authors of providing a justification for attacks on dams.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's chief negotiator, described the report on X on Tuesday as “setting the stage for the next round of attacks on civilian infrastructure.”

“Well, new rule: We apply your own logic in the same way,” he wrote. “Any dam, port, or power plant located near an American or Israeli base has a dual use.”
